angle: We thought we knew our ICP. Our closed-won data said otherwise
linkedin_post:
Our ICP was wrong.

Not completely wrong. But the closed-won data told a different story than the one we'd been telling ourselves.

We assumed our ICP was pretty standard: the usual top segments, the usual types of businesses we sell into.

Then we looked back at our closed-won customers and dug into the conversation transcripts from those deals. We were hunting for specific moments that kept showing up.

One of them was a recent product launch. When a company had just launched a product, they were looking at Unify at a higher clip.

That's not a firmographic. You won't find it in a segment filter on company size or industry. It's a moment, and you only see it when you read what buyers actually said.

Most teams define ICP once, from a whiteboard, and then never test it against who actually buys.

Your closed-won deals are already telling you who your buyer is and when they show up. The transcripts are sitting in your call recorder.

When did you last compare your ICP to your closed-won data?

lesson.title: Let closed-won data rewrite your ICP
takeaways: An assumed ICP is a hypothesis, and closed-won deals are how you test it.
Call transcripts reveal moments, like a recent product launch, that firmographics miss.
Buyers with a specific recent event can show interest in your product at a higher clip.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last 10 closed-won deals, read the call transcripts, and list any moment or event that shows up in more than one. Compare that list to your current ICP definition.

angle: How to launch an automated outbound play without sending anything embarrassing
post_first_line: Delay your first send by 10 minutes.
linkedin_post:
Delay your first send by 10 minutes.

That one setting is how I launch an automated play without sending anything embarrassing.

When a new play goes live, I hold the sequence for around 10 to 20 minutes. Delaying a sequence is something you can do natively in Unify.

Then I read through the sample emails and check for accuracy. I'm making sure nothing wacky is going out.

By that point we've already tested the agents and the snippets at a smaller scale. The delay is the last check before volume.

If a sample shows something off, like a reply saying we didn't launch that product, or a reference to something from months ago, I tweak the agent and keep testing.

And there will be edge cases. We'll probably get one every few thousand emails.

Based on the success we've seen, it's well worth it.

The goal isn't a perfect launch. It's catching the obvious problems before they hit thousands of inboxes.

What's your last check before launching a play?

Slide 4: Read the sample emails and check for accuracy

Slide 8: It's well worth it based on the success

lesson.title: Launching an automated outbound play safely
takeaways: Test agents and snippets at a smaller scale before going wide.
Delay the first send by 10 to 20 minutes so you can review sample emails.
When a sample is off, tweak the agent and keep testing rather than pausing the whole play.
lesson.exercise: Before your next play goes live, add a 10 to 20 minute delay to the sequence and review a handful of sample emails for accuracy, outdated references, and anything odd.

angle: Our AI signal kept flagging pricing changes as 'major launches.' Here's the fix.
post_first_line: Pricing changes are not major launches.
linkedin_post:
Pricing changes are not major launches.

My AI signal kept getting this wrong, and the fix was simpler than I expected.

While testing it early on, I noticed it was pulling in a lot of lighter announcements that we wouldn't consider launches. Pricing changes. Internal tools. Internal hiring news.

The problem was that I never defined what a "major launch" actually meant. The model filled in the blanks on its own.

So I gave it specific criteria and structure.

What counts: a major feature, a significant go-to-market shift, or a net new customer-facing product.

What gets ignored: pricing-only announcements and similar lighter news.

Same model, same data. The only change was a clearer definition of what counts and what doesn't.

If your signal is noisy, the prompt is usually the first place to look. Tell it what to include, and be just as explicit about what to ignore.

What's the noisiest signal in your workflow right now?
carousel: Slide 1: My AI signal kept flagging pricing changes as major launches
Slide 2: In testing, it pulled in pricing updates, internal tools, and hiring news
Slide 3: The model wasn't broken. I never defined 'major launch.'
Slide 4: Fix one: spell out what counts as a major launch
Slide 5: A major feature, a big go-to-market shift, a net new customer-facing product
Slide 6: Fix two: spell out what to ignore, like pricing-only announcements
Slide 7: Same model, same data, far less noise
Slide 8: Vague criteria in means noisy signals out

lesson.title: Define 'major' before your AI does it for you
takeaways: Vague terms like 'major launch' get interpreted loosely by the model, which creates noise.
Early testing surfaces false positives such as pricing changes, internal tools, and hiring news.
Explicit include and exclude criteria give the signal structure to work from.
lesson.exercise: Pick one AI signal you run. List 5 recent false positives, then rewrite the prompt with a clear 'counts as' list and an 'ignore' list, and rerun it.

angle: The buying signals we watch when the real pain isn't public
post_first_line: Hiring a ton for BD means pipeline pain.
linkedin_post:
Hiring a ton for BD means pipeline pain.

That's one of the signals I watch when a company's real problem isn't public.

Nobody posts "our pipeline is broken" on their website. So I infer it from what they do instead.

Hiring a lot for the BD team? They probably need more pipeline.

Then I read inside the job description. It gives a sense of their tech stack, which shows their current workflow and the potential pains to go after.

Headcount growth is another signal. So is divestment in certain areas.

What counts will look different depending on the type of business. But the pattern holds: a lot of external signals, and inferring from there.

angle: Spotting the signal is only half the job. The other half is the message
post_first_line: Intent signals only solve half the problem.
linkedin_post:
Intent signals only solve half the problem.

The other half is what happens after the signal fires.

Quintin Smith made a point worth calling out: the power comes from two things working together. First, taking signals and using them as intent triggers for specific plays, with always-on monitoring behind them.

Second, customizing the copy for each of those plays.

Most teams stop at the first part. They spot the signal, then a seller has to go build the message by hand.

That's where the manual work creeps back in. A seller looks at the intent signal, then writes the outreach from scratch.

Quintin's point is that both pieces can be automated. The action follows the trigger, and the outreach is personalized to be hyper relevant at scale.

So nobody has to customize every single message, and nobody has to interpret every signal.

A great signal with generic copy is still a generic email.

Where does your signal-to-message handoff break down?
carousel: Slide 1: Spotting the signal is only half the job.
Slide 2: The other half is the message that follows.
Slide 3: Signals can trigger specific plays through always-on monitoring.
Slide 4: Most teams stop there and hand off to a seller.
Slide 5: Then the seller builds the copy by hand.
Slide 6: Quintin Smith: automate the trigger and the copy.
Slide 7: Outreach becomes hyper relevant at scale.
Slide 8: A great signal with generic copy is still generic.

lesson.title: Automate the Signal and the Message
takeaways: Intent signals work best as triggers for specific plays, monitored always-on.
Personalized copy is the second half of the job, not an afterthought.
Automating both the trigger and the copy removes manual seller work and keeps outreach relevant at scale.
lesson.exercise: Map one intent signal you track today. Write down what action it triggers and who writes the message. If a person writes it by hand every time, draft a template that adapts to that signal.
